name: migrations
description: Which schema version the database is at. Both implementations read the same database, so both need the same answer to 'is this schema new enough for me'.

columns.name: version
columns.description: The migration number. The highest row is the current schema version.
columns.note: Legacy declares it with @PrimaryGeneratedColumn and says in a comment that it is not actually a primary column — the value comes from the migration file name, not from the database.

columns.name: file_name
columns.note: Legacy declares no explicit column name, so TypeORM's default applies and the column is fileName in camelCase — unlike every other table here. Confirm against the live schema before generating DDL.

notes: The version is what lets a process refuse to start against a schema it does not understand. That refusal is shared behavior, not infrastructure: if the TypeScript backend starts against an old schema and the fast path does not, the disagreement is a bug — which is the test contracts/AGENTS.md sets for inclusion.
Timestamps are UTC milliseconds; see types/Timestamp.json. Legacy uses datetime without precision(3).

open.question: Does gradido2 keep this table, and does the fast path write to it?
open.detail: Migrations are numbered files in legacy and the table is their bookkeeping. gradido2 may pick a different mechanism entirely. What must be decided either way is which process is allowed to migrate — if both implementations may, two of them starting at once race on the same schema — and what a process does when it finds a version it does not know: refuse, or run read-only.
open.why_it_matters: It is the first thing both implementations touch on startup and the one place where they can destroy each other's assumptions.
open.status: unanswered — decide before the second implementation opens the database
